Sixth grade science · Unit 5

Plate Tectonics & Rocks

The ground under your feet is a moving puzzle floating on slow-flowing rock. It built the Himalayas, shakes California, and made the stones in your driveway. Michigan's Great Lakes are the work of a one-mile-thick wall of ice. Let's see how it all fits together.

Where we left off: Unit 4 followed the Sun's energy through air and water. Earth has a second energy source: heat from deep inside. You may already have learned about convection, rising warm material and sinking cool material. The same idea, in very slow motion, moves the plates, and the forces from Unit 3 are what push, pull, and bend rock.

Concept 1 · Inside Earth

Earth has layers

Earth is built in layers: a thin crust, a thick flowing mantle, a liquid outer core, and a solid inner core. It gets hotter and more squeezed the deeper you go.

Analogy

A peach

Earth's crust is only about 0.5% of the way to the center: thinner relative to the planet than a peach skin is to the peach. Under it the mantle is a thick layer of hot rock that moves very slowly.

Where it breaks: a peach is solid all the way through. Earth's mantle flows like extremely thick syrup, and the core is mostly iron, not fruit.

Try it

Drill down

Predict. Imagine digging straight down 6,371 km to the center of Earth. Will it get hotter or colder? Which layer do you think is thickest? Is the very center solid or liquid?

Do. Drag the depth slider from 0 to the bottom in steps. Stop near 35 km, 2,890 km, and 5,150 km and read the layer name, temperature, and pressure.

Notice. The crust is a thin skin (about 35 km on average here) compared with the mantle underneath. The temperature and pressure keep rising with depth. The outer core is liquid; the inner core is solid even though it is the hottest, because the pressure is so high.

Why it matters. We have never drilled through the crust. Everything we know about the layers comes from how earthquake waves travel through Earth. The moving layers are why we have volcanoes, earthquakes, and mountains.

Data

Temperature climbs with depth

Approximate values. We have barely scratched the skin of the planet. The deepest mines go down about 4 km (2.5 miles), and the deepest hole ever drilled (Kola, Russia) reached only 12 km (7.5 miles), about 0.2% of the way to the center. Even that far down the rock is hot: deep gold mines in South Africa have rock around 60 °C and need giant air conditioners, and the bottom of the Kola hole was already about 180 °C. The deeper you go, the hotter it gets, because Earth's inside is still hot from when the planet formed, and natural radioactive atoms in the rock keep adding heat. Near the center it is about 5,400 °C.

Concept 2 · Moving plates

The ground is a slow puzzle

Earth's crust and top of the mantle break into plates that creep a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow. Over millions of years they carried one giant continent, Pangaea, apart into the continents we know. Plates meet at three kinds of boundaries.

Try it

Drag back in time: where the continents were

The big claim: about 250 million years ago nearly all of Earth's land was joined into one supercontinent called Pangaea. Drag the slider back in time to watch the continents come together. Use the thin black country borders to find places you know.

Maps: PALEOMAP Project reconstructions by C. R. Scotese and others (“Mollweide Paleographic Map of Earth,” ages 5, 60, 105, 155, 190, 225 and 250 million years), via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. Thin black lines are today's country borders, drawn so you can find places. Light blue is shallow sea. The farther back in time, the less certain the reconstruction, and the first map is 5 million years ago, not exactly today. This is a Mollweide (oval) projection, so shapes near the edges look squeezed.

Analogy

The skin on hot pudding

Hot pudding grows a thin skin on top. Underneath, the pudding churns in slow loops because the bottom is hotter than the top, and those loops drag the skin along. The skin cracks into pieces that drift apart, bump together, and sometimes crumple. Earth's plates are the pieces of skin, and the hot rock of the mantle is the pudding. It is the same idea as the convection you learned in Unit 2.

Where it breaks: pudding is a runny liquid and its skin moves in seconds. The mantle is solid rock that flows only a few centimeters a year, and the plates are about 100 kilometers thick.

Diagram

Three kinds of boundaries

Try it

Watch the Atlantic open

Diagram

Evidence the continents fit together

The claim: South America and Africa used to be one piece. The evidence: slide the control back in time and watch the clues line up.

Simplified shapes, not to scale. Real evidence: coastlines fit, the same fossils (the freshwater reptile Mesosaurus, the fern Glossopteris) appear on both sides of the ocean, matching rock types and mountain ranges, and glacier scratches that line up.

Data

How fast do plates move?

Plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow: a few centimeters a year, an inch or two. That sounds like nothing, but plates never stop. In your lifetime a plate moves about 2.5 meters, about the length of a small car. In a million years it moves about 40 kilometers, around 25 miles. Over 100 million years that adds up to thousands of kilometers, enough to open an entire ocean. Scientists can measure it today with GPS stations bolted to every major plate.

Typical speeds in centimeters per year. Your fingernails grow about 4 cm a year.

Concept 3 · Earthquakes and volcanoes

What happens at the edges

Plates snag on each other, stress builds, then they suddenly slip: an earthquake. Where one plate sinks, the water it carries down helps melt the rock above it, and the magma rises: a volcano. Most of both happen along plate boundaries.

Analogy

A stuck book, and a shaken soda

Stick and slip

Pull a book with a rubber band. It sticks, the band stretches, then it jerks. That jerk is an earthquake.

Shaken soda

Gas dissolved in magma expands as it rises and blasts out like opening a shaken soda.

Pushed rug

Push two edges of a rug together and it bunches into a ridge. Colliding plates do this to make mountains.

Try it

Build up stress, trigger a quake

Push again and again. Nobody knows exactly when it will slip, or which way.

Diagram

A subduction zone

The sinking plate drags water down. Water lowers the melting point of the hot rock above it, magma forms, and it rises. This is how the Pacific Ring of Fire gets its volcanoes.

Real world

The Ring of Fire

Most of the world's earthquakes and volcanoes are not scattered at random. They line up along plate boundaries. The biggest line circles the Pacific Ocean like a horseshoe, and it is called the Ring of Fire.

Look first: What do you notice about where these volcanoes are? Think about it (or talk it over) before you turn on any more layers.

Volcano that has erupted since 1700Earthquake of magnitude 7 or more since 1900Plates collidePlates pull apartPlates slide past

The Ring of Fire is about 40,000 km (25,000 miles) around and holds roughly 3 of every 4 of Earth's volcanoes and about 9 of every 10 of its earthquakes. Volcano locations: NOAA National Centers for Environmental Information. Earthquakes: U.S. Geological Survey. Plate boundaries and coastlines: Müller and others (2019) plate model, CC BY 4.0.

Data

Big quakes are rare. Small ones are everywhere.

Approximate yearly worldwide counts (USGS-style rounded). Each whole step up in magnitude is about 10 times fewer quakes but about 32 times more energy released.

Concept 4 · The rock cycle

Rocks recycle

Rocks slowly change from one type to another: igneous (cooled magma), sedimentary (squeezed pieces), metamorphic (changed by heat and pressure). No rock is permanent.

Analogy

Crayons

Real rock: basalt, an igneous rock that cooled from lava. Photo: Mike Davis (GeoDIL), CC0, Wikimedia Commons.

Melt and cool = igneous

Melt a crayon and let it harden. Same idea as lava or magma cooling.

Real rock: sandstone layers in Zion National Park, Utah, a sedimentary rock. Photo: Nhartmannphotos, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Shavings pressed = sedimentary

Pack crayon shavings in layers and press. Bits of old rock get squeezed into layers.

Real rock: garnet gneiss from the Adirondack Mountains, New York, a metamorphic rock with bands. Photo: Shannon Heinle (GeoDIL), CC0, Wikimedia Commons.

Warm and squish = metamorphic

Warm a crayon and squeeze it. It changes shape and swirl without melting. Pressure and heat change rocks without melting them.

Real rocks take thousands to millions of years; a crayon takes minutes. The photos show the real rocks each crayon step stands for.

Where it breaks: squeezed crayon shavings stick because wax is soft. Sedimentary rock is cemented by minerals over a long time, and metamorphic rock usually recrystallizes into new minerals instead of just bending.

Try it

Take a rock on a journey

Predict. Pick a rock, say granite. Where could it be in a million years? Can any rock turn into any other rock? How many steps would it take to get back to granite?

Do. Start as igneous rock. Each time you press a button you choose what happens to the rock next. Keep going for at least six steps and read the log. Try to visit all four stages.

Notice. Every stage has more than one exit, but magma can only cool into igneous rock. A rock can also loop back to the same type (new sedimentary rock from old). There is no start and no finish and no single "correct" path.

Why it matters. Rock is never used up, only changed. The cycle takes millions of years and runs on two engines: Earth's heat from the inside (melting, squeezing) and the Sun-driven water and wind at the surface (weathering, erosion).

Data

Cool slowly = big crystals

Photos: obsidian, James St. John (CC BY 2.0); basalt, Mike Davis (CC0); granite, James St. John (CC BY 2.0). All via Wikimedia Commons.

Concept 5 · Shaping the surface

Break, carry, drop

Weathering breaks rock into pieces, erosion carries the pieces away, and deposition drops them somewhere new. Water, wind, and ice do the work.

Analogy

A grater, a conveyor belt, and a dump truck

Three different jobs, often happening at once. Weathering is the grater: it breaks big rock into small pieces. Erosion is the conveyor belt: water, wind, or ice carries the pieces away. Deposition is the dump truck: the load stops moving and piles up. A river can do all three in one bend: it grinds rock, carries sand, and drops it on the inside bank.

Where it breaks: real erosion has no separate machines. One storm can weather, carry, and dump in the same hour.

Diagram

A bending river

The river slowly swings sideways as it carves one bank and builds the other.

Try it

Watch a river change course

A river does not stay put. On every bend the fast water eats the outside bank and the slow water drops sand on the inside, so each bend creeps sideways and grows into a loop. Over decades to centuries the neck of a loop can get so thin that the river breaks through and takes a shortcut. The old loop is left behind as a curved pond called an oxbow lake.

Real rivers that moved

The drawing above is a simple model. Real rivers do the same thing, and big ones move a lot over centuries and thousands of years. Here are three real records.

Try it

Fast water vs. slow water

Simplified minimum speeds. Fast floods move boulders; slow lakes only settle clay. That is why the sediment in a delta is sorted by size.

Try it

Watch the ice come and go

For tens of thousands of years, ice sheets grew and melted over Michigan. Drag the slider to see where the edge of the ice was, and when it left each place.

The ice edge uses the "optimal" estimate from the North American Deglacial Isochrones (NADI-1; Dalton and others, 2020, 2023; CC BY 4.0), in calendar years before today. Dates are approximate, and the real edge moved back and forth. Today's lakes are drawn for orientation; while the ice melted, the meltwater formed bigger, different lakes.

Build it

Engineering challenge: the riverbank guard

The problem: protect a sand riverbank from washing away when water is poured down the same slope that erodes an unprotected bank.

Criteria: less sand collects at the bottom than from the unprotected bank, using the same amount of water both times.

Constraints: rocks from the yard rock collection, sticks, or other small objects pressed into the sand. No glue or tape, and no reshaping the slope itself.

  1. Try it in the game first. Play Rock Cycle Router at the bottom of this page. Notice which moves are weathering and which are erosion.
  2. Plan. Sketch two different ideas on your design log. Label how each one slows the water down or blocks it from carrying sand away.
  3. Build and test. Pour the same amount of water down the unprotected bank first and collect the sand that washes off. Then test your protected bank the same way, with a clean collection cup.
  4. Improve. Change one thing, test again, and record it.

Print a design log for each team. This is the same problem as a real levee or breakwater: slow the water, and it drops its sediment instead of carrying it away.

Check yourself

Can you explain it?

Explain why Michigan has no volcanoes but lots of sand dunes and boulders, and how a rock could end up as marble.

Show a model answer

Michigan is in the middle of a plate, far from the boundaries where plates collide or pull apart, so there are no volcanoes and few earthquakes. Instead, its surface was reshaped by glaciers that ground up rock and carried boulders (weathering, erosion, deposition), and wind and waves still move sand into dunes.

Limestone is a sedimentary rock made of shells and mud pressed together. If heat and pressure from plate collisions change it without melting, it becomes marble, a metamorphic rock.

Words to know

crust
Earth's thin, rocky outer layer.
mantle
Thick layer of hot, slowly flowing rock under the crust.
core
Iron-nickel center: liquid outside, solid inside.
plate
A giant slab of crust and upper mantle.
boundary
Where two plates meet.
earthquake
Shaking when plates suddenly slip.
magma
Molten rock underground. It is called lava on the surface.
igneous rock
Formed from cooled magma or lava.
sedimentary rock
Formed from squeezed layers of sediment.
metamorphic rock
Changed by heat and pressure without melting.
weathering
Breaking rock into smaller pieces.
erosion
Moving broken pieces from place to place.
deposition
Dropping the carried pieces.
Tutor notes: hands-on kit, misconceptions, pacing

Kit (about $10): a hard-boiled egg, modeling clay in layers, crayons and a grater, a toaster or warm water bath (adult-supervised) for melting, graham crackers and frosting, sandpaper, a stream table made from a baking tray with sand, a rock collection from the yard.

  • Concept 1: crack a hard-boiled egg: shell = crust, white = mantle, yolk = core. Cut a layered clay ball in half.
  • Concept 2: push graham crackers on frosting: apart (divergent), together (convergent), sideways (transform).
  • Concept 3: pull a rubber-banded book across a table until it jerks. Shake and open a soda outdoors.
  • Concept 4: grate crayon shavings, press and warm gently between wax paper; melt a crayon to compare.
  • Concept 5: tilt a tray of sand and pour water at different speeds. Sort the deposits by size. Then run the riverbank guard challenge (about 30 to 40 minutes), reusing the stream table and rock collection already in the kit.

Common misconceptions:

  • "Earth's mantle is liquid." It's solid rock that flows very slowly.
  • "Continents float on water." They are parts of plates riding on hot, soft rock.
  • "Metamorphic rocks are melted." If melted, they'd become igneous.
  • "Earthquakes can be predicted exactly." We know where, not exactly when.

Pacing: about five 30-minute sessions.

After the lesson · Game

Play: Rock Cycle Router

Turn one rock into another using real processes: melting, cooling, weathering, burial, and heat and pressure. Each move only works in the right place. Find the shortest route.
